Example and follow-up
The caller may see five permitted orders while count reveals 900 hidden orders. Test zero-access users, count-only requests, filters, ordering and navigation. If the provider cannot securely support a requested aggregate or filter, reject it under a documented contract instead of returning a misleading result.

Avoid this mistake
Filtering only the displayed page leaves count, aggregates and existence checks exposed.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do you handle count-only requests?
  • What if the remote API cannot apply your authorization predicate?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses one authorized result definition
  • Protects count and aggregates
  • Rejects unsupported semantics explicitly
Verification evidence
Use restricted identities and compare authorized data, count and aggregate responses over the same fixture.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Requesting and Setting Data or Count
    Handle data and count requests independently. Apply the same authorization and filtering to both; test count-only requests.

column1: MODEL-04 | A query-provider filter cannot be converted to simple ranges. A developer catches the exception and returns everything. What is the correction?
column2:
Short answer
Preserve the requested Boolean semantics or reject the unsupported filter clearly. Range conversion is not a universal representation of arbitrary nested AND/OR expressions and functions. Use a supported expression representation or another safe translation strategy appropriate to the provider. Combine user filters with mandatory authorization predicates independently, so a parsing failure cannot remove either restriction. Validate dynamic identifiers and values through supported APIs.

Example and follow-up
Consider (region=A AND amount>100) OR (region=B AND urgent=true). Flattening this into independent region and amount ranges changes the result. Build fixtures that distinguish the intended expression from the flattened one, and include an unsupported-function request.

Avoid this mistake
A swallowed filter exception must not become an unrestricted selection.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Can the backend express the same predicate?
  • How do mandatory authorization filters survive translation failure?
Strong answer criteria
  • Preserves AND/OR grouping
  • Separates mandatory restrictions
  • Returns an explicit unsupported-request outcome
Verification evidence
Compare expected row sets for nested filters and prove failure never broadens authorized access.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Implementing Filtering in an Unmanaged Query
    Check supported filter representations and conversion limitations. Unsupported input must not remove required user or authorization restrictions.

column1: MODEL-05 | A paged custom entity repeats some rows after an insertion. How would you make the contract predictable?
column2:
Short answer
Start with deterministic ordering that includes a unique tie-breaker; sorting only by a nonunique date is insufficient. Then distinguish deterministic order from snapshot consistency: concurrent inserts can still shift offset pages. Choose the supported continuation or consistency mechanism, or document the weaker browsing behavior if a snapshot is unnecessary. For an export requiring completeness, design a stable extraction boundary rather than assuming UI paging is a reliable bulk-transfer protocol.

Example and follow-up
Twenty orders share a creation date. A new order is inserted between page requests. Test tied values, reverse sorting, deleted rows, empty pages and a count change. State whether the product requires an interactive current list or a reproducible export.

Avoid this mistake
Adding ORDER BY alone does not guarantee a frozen dataset across requests.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is the tie-breaker?
  • Does the use case require a snapshot or just stable ordering?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates ordering from consistency
  • Chooses a contract for concurrent changes
  • Tests page boundaries with duplicate sort values
Verification evidence
Run successive requests while inserting and deleting records and verify the documented paging behavior.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Interface IF_RAP_QUERY_PAGING
    Distinguish offset, zero page size and PAGE_SIZE_UNLIMITED. The paging interface does not itself provide a cross-request snapshot.

column1: MODEL-06 | Adding a language-dependent text association doubles order totals. Would DISTINCT be a good fix?
column2:
Short answer
First identify the grain of the result and the actual join multiplicity. Check language, validity and other conditions that make the text association to-one or to-many. Declared cardinality is not data cleanup and can mislead optimization when false. Repair the relationship or aggregate at the correct grain before exposing the measure. DISTINCT can mask the symptom while retaining incorrect totals or discarding legitimate detail.

Example and follow-up
One order worth 100 EUR joins two text rows and contributes 200 EUR to a sum. Add overlapping validity periods to the fixture as well as two languages. Verify both the detailed entity and the consuming analytical or list result.

Avoid this mistake
Do not fix an incorrect join by simply declaring a to-one cardinality.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is one row supposed to represent?
  • Which data condition establishes uniqueness?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines result grain
  • Proves association multiplicity
  • Checks the downstream measure
Verification evidence
Show expected rows and totals for multiple texts, missing texts and overlapping validity intervals.

Read and verify
  • SAP CDS modeling course
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-07 | A CDS report sums 100 EUR and 100 USD into 200. What should the model and service do?
column2:
Short answer
Preserve amount/currency and quantity/unit semantics throughout the model. A sum is meaningful only within compatible units or after an explicitly defined conversion. Decide the target currency, rate type, date and rounding policy with the business owner. An annotation communicates semantics but does not, by itself, perform a correct conversion or make arbitrary aggregation valid. Verify how the actual analytical or transactional consumer interprets the exposed fields.

Example and follow-up
Provide mixed currencies, a missing exchange rate and a value requiring rounding. A summary can group by currency or apply approved conversion, but must not silently combine incomparable values. Keep original values available where reconciliation requires them.

Avoid this mistake
Do not confuse semantic annotations with conversion logic.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which date determines the rate?
  • At which stage is rounding applied?
Strong answer criteria
  • Maintains unit semantics
  • Names the business conversion policy
  • Reconciles rounded and original values
Verification evidence
Compare expected totals for same-currency, mixed-currency and missing-rate fixtures.

Read and verify
  • SAP CDS modeling course
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-08 | A transactional projection needs a calculated field that its provider contract does not permit. How do you redesign it?
column2:
Short answer
Check the exact projection/provider-contract restrictions in the target release. Place permitted calculations in an appropriate underlying data model, expose a suitable read model, or use a supported virtual-element mechanism when its limitations fit. Do not turn a transactional projection into an arbitrary join solely to satisfy the UI. Preserve stable identity, behavior mapping, authorization and update semantics across the chosen design.

Example and follow-up
The UI requests a derived risk band and wants to filter by it. A transient calculation may display correctly but fail server-side filtering. Decide whether the risk belongs in persistent business state, a database expression or a read-only enrichment, and test that consumer requirement.

Avoid this mistake
A field that displays in preview is not proof of a supported filterable transactional contract.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Does the field participate in filtering or ordering?
  • Who owns recalculation when source data changes?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks the provider contract
  • Preserves transactional identity
  • Designs for consumer query semantics
Verification evidence
Exercise read, filter, order and update against the intended binding on the target release.

Read and verify
  • SAP CDS modeling course
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-09 | The business wants to sort a million-row list by a virtual element computed through a remote call. What would you propose?
column2:
Short answer
Challenge the requested access pattern before implementing row-by-row enrichment. A virtual element does not automatically support efficient database sorting, filtering or aggregation. Consider a permitted persistent read model with refresh rules, a supported pushdown calculation, or a bounded enrichment where sorting is not required. State freshness, failure and reconciliation requirements. Avoid moving an unbounded database workload into ABAP or remote calls.

Example and follow-up
A risk score depends on a remote provider. Define how stale it may be and what the UI shows when the provider is unavailable. Compare query latency and result correctness with representative volumes; a fast demo using ten rows does not establish scalability.

Avoid this mistake
Do not claim that adding a virtual element automatically pushes its logic to HANA.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What freshness is acceptable?
  • How many remote calls occur for one page and its count?
Strong answer criteria
  • Identifies unsupported query operations
  • Controls remote-call volume
  • Makes freshness and failure explicit
Verification evidence
Measure request count, rows transferred and latency with a realistic dataset and a failing remote dependency.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP: implementing sorting of virtual elements
    Explains transformation of supported virtual-element sort requests before retrieval. Verify projection, protocol, interface release and consumer restrictions on the target release.

column1: MODEL-10 | Two rows in a service share the declared CDS key after a join. Why is this more than a display issue?
column2:
Short answer
Consumer identity must uniquely and stably distinguish each exposed instance. Declaring an element as key does not make a nonunique SQL result unique. Duplicate identities can corrupt navigation, client caching, selection and mutation targeting. Correct the data grain, join or composite key while assessing compatibility for existing consumers. If the current public identity is wrong, plan an explicit API transition rather than silently changing key meaning.

Example and follow-up
An order-item service exposes only OrderId as key. Two items appear with the same identity and the UI targets the wrong item. Test read-by-key and navigation, not merely row count. Include repeated reads in different orders to reveal unstable client behavior.

Avoid this mistake
Do not hide duplicate-key rows with client-side deduplication.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Can the public key change compatibly?
  • Is the entity a business object instance or an aggregate?
Strong answer criteria
  • Proves key uniqueness at exposed grain
  • Explains consumer consequences
  • Plans compatible identity evolution
Verification evidence
Validate uniqueness, stable canonical URLs and correct read/update targeting for multiple child records.

Read and verify
  • SAP CDS modeling course
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-11 | A value help reveals customer names that the order list hides. Where should the fix live?
column2:
Short answer
Treat the value-help entity and its text/navigation paths as separately consumed data contracts. Apply the required access restrictions and validate actual user identity and context. UI annotations can connect a value help but do not establish its authorization. Ensure the selected value is still validated at the write boundary because clients can submit a value without using the UI chooser.

Example and follow-up
A restricted user opens customer search and learns names outside their organization. Test direct access to the value-help service, search/count behavior and a forged customer value in an order update. The read restriction and business consistency check solve related but distinct problems.

Avoid this mistake
Hiding the value-help control is not a backend security fix.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Can the entity be consumed directly?
  • What checks a value submitted outside Fiori?
Strong answer criteria
  • Protects auxiliary data exposure
  • Checks direct service access
  • Validates proposed business references
Verification evidence
Execute denied-user searches and direct payload changes using allowed and forbidden customer keys.

Read and verify
  • SAP Learning: authority checks and DCL
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-12 | A batch job asks to use privileged EML because normal authorization rejects it. How do you evaluate the request?
column2:
Short answer
First establish the job identity, its legitimate business scope and whether normal authorization can represent that scope. Privileged access is a provider-enabled contract with specific bypass behavior, not a generic workaround. Review the defined authorization contexts, exposed entry points and caller trust boundary. If privilege is justified, narrowly encapsulate it, preserve remaining business checks and produce auditable evidence of who requested which effect.

Example and follow-up
A repair job should reconcile one approved organizational scope, not become an unrestricted posting API. Test both the approved job path and attempts to reach the helper from an ordinary consumer. Confirm which checks are bypassed in the actual provider contract.

Avoid this mistake
Do not assume PRIVILEGED, IN LOCAL MODE and a technical user are equivalent.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which authorization context is disabled?
  • Why cannot ordinary scoped authorization satisfy the requirement?
Strong answer criteria
  • Requires a provider-supported privilege contract
  • Limits the trusted entry point
  • Retains business checks and auditability
Verification evidence
Review privilege configuration and demonstrate allowed repair plus rejected unauthorized invocation.

Read and verify
  • SAP EML local and privileged modes
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-13 | A developer uses IN LOCAL MODE in a helper to avoid feature checks. What makes the helper safe or unsafe?
column2:
Short answer
Locate the helper within its own BO implementation and trace every public operation that can reach it. Local mode supports internal state maintenance and bypasses defined checks depending on the operation; it does not authorize arbitrary external business requests or erase transactional constraints. Ensure public inputs have already been checked and that internal changes preserve invariants. Review cross-BO calls under their own contracts.

Example and follow-up
A determination legitimately updates a derived readonly amount. The same helper becomes unsafe if a public action forwards arbitrary caller values to it. Test that the derived field cannot be controlled indirectly through a newly added action parameter.

Avoid this mistake
Do not fix missing authorization by routing all work through local mode.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which controls does this specific operation bypass?
  • Can a caller influence the supposedly derived values?
Strong answer criteria
  • Traces trust from public input
  • Confines internal state changes
  • Distinguishes own-BO and cross-BO access
Verification evidence
Use adversarial action inputs and verify that only approved derivations reach readonly or protected fields.

Read and verify
  • SAP EML local and privileged modes
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-14 | A CDS unit test passes, but the same entity leaks data for a restricted user. What may the test be missing?
column2:
Short answer
Inspect the test environment and access-control configuration. A test focused on relational logic with CDS doubles may intentionally isolate or disable access control; it is not automatically an authorization test. Enable the supported access-control testing mechanism with meaningful role data where available, and add real service tests under restricted identities. Keep query-correctness evidence separate from security evidence.

Example and follow-up
One test proves the join returns three rows. Add fixtures for no authorization and two distinct scopes, then ensure the test actually evaluates DCL. A final service test also verifies binding, identity propagation and the real consumed entity.

Avoid this mistake
A green database-double test does not prove deployed authorization.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Is DCL enabled in the test environment?
  • Which real identity is used by the service?
Strong answer criteria
  • Inspects double behavior
  • Adds denied and scoped authorization cases
  • Separates unit and deployed evidence
Verification evidence
Show test configuration plus restricted-user service results; do not infer one from the other.

Read and verify
  • SAP CDS access-control tests
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-15 | An integration user can access all tenants or clients through a custom read provider. What boundaries must be reviewed?
column2:
Short answer
Separate technical client handling, tenant isolation, business authorization and remote credentials. Standard data-access behavior does not automatically protect arbitrary remote calls or custom assembled datasets. Avoid accepting unrestricted client/tenant selectors from untrusted request input. Use supported tenant-aware access and configuration, enforce business scope and test identity propagation. The exact tenant model differs by environment and must be established explicitly.

Example and follow-up
A provider forwards an incoming company or tenant parameter to a privileged remote destination. Even if the local CDS looks restricted, the remote response may cross the intended boundary. Test two scopes with overlapping business IDs and inspect both request construction and returned data.

Avoid this mistake
Do not treat a client field, a destination name or authentication alone as complete tenant isolation.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Who controls the remote tenant selector?
  • Which identity does the remote system evaluate?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates technical and business scope
  • Constrains untrusted selectors
  • Checks end-to-end identity propagation
Verification evidence
Run cross-scope negative tests and review the permitted communication configuration without exposing secrets.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP authorization control
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-16 | A projection hides an operation, but another consumer can still call the base BO. Is hiding sufficient?
column2:
Short answer
Projection restrictions define a consumer-facing operation surface, not a universal revocation of the underlying capability. Review who can consume the base BO or another released interface, and enforce security at the appropriate behavior boundary. Keep public API release, package visibility and operation authorization aligned. Feature control can improve availability feedback but cannot replace authorization for alternative entry points.

Example and follow-up
A UI projection excludes Delete while a background consumer uses a broader local BO interface. Decide whether that capability is intentional for the background role. Test direct access to every supported mutation path using an unauthorized identity.

Avoid this mistake
Do not use the UI service shape as the only security policy.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which consumers are permitted to use the base contract?
  • Where does the decisive permission check execute?
Strong answer criteria
  • Inventories alternate entry points
  • Separates surface restriction from permission
  • Tests local and remote consumers
Verification evidence
Provide a consumer/operation/identity matrix and evidence of denied mutation through each exposed path.

Read and verify
  • SAP BO interfaces
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-17 | A released entity gains a new field that is expensive and sensitive. Is an additive change automatically safe?
column2:
Short answer
Not necessarily. Check default projection, serialization, authorization, query cost and consumers that interpret metadata or request broad selections. Preserve compatibility while deciding whether the field belongs in the same public contract or a more restricted projection. Avoid unexpected remote enrichment or large payload growth on existing list requests. Verify the relevant release contract and supported evolution rules before shipping.

Example and follow-up
A new personal-data field is included by broad selects and exports. Another computed field adds one remote call per row. Existing callers did not change, but privacy and latency did. Test default reads, explicit selection, metadata-driven UIs and restricted identities.

Avoid this mistake
Do not assess compatibility using only whether old source code still compiles.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Does an existing broad select expose it?
  • How does it affect authorization and request cost?
Strong answer criteria
  • Assesses semantic and operational compatibility
  • Controls default exposure
  • Tests unchanged consumers
Verification evidence
Compare old/new payloads, access results and latency for representative existing requests.

Read and verify
  • SAP BO interfaces
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: MODEL-18 | An analytical requirement is added to a transactional BO. Would you put every aggregate into its projection?
column2:
Short answer
Choose a read model appropriate to the analytical grain and consumer rather than distorting transactional identity and behavior. Reuse trustworthy underlying semantics where suitable, then define aggregation, currency, authorization and freshness deliberately. Keep transactional mutations on the BO contract. A separate analytical model may be justified, but avoid duplicating business rules without an ownership and consistency plan.

Example and follow-up
An approval object needs both item editing and monthly spend by organization. The monthly aggregate is not the same entity identity as an editable item. Compare whether live calculation meets latency or whether a reconciled read model is necessary.

Avoid this mistake
Do not make an aggregate writable merely because its source is a transactional BO.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is the aggregate grain?
  • How are authorization and currency preserved across the models?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates transaction and analytical identity
  • Reuses semantics intentionally
  • Defines freshness and reconciliation
Verification evidence
Reconcile grouped totals to authorized transactional fixtures and validate the intended analytical consumer.

Read and verify
  • SAP analytical projection modeling
    Verify the actual consumption path and include denied-user, filtering and boundary tests.

column1: OPS-01 | How would you test a Submit action without replacing the business object you are supposed to verify?
column2:
Short answer
Keep the Submit implementation and its relevant BO behavior real. Isolate true dependencies such as database tables, external service adapters or other BOs using the appropriate supported doubles. Drive the operation through a meaningful boundary, often EML, and assert state changes, failures and messages. A double of the very action under test would prove the configured double response rather than the business rule.

Example and follow-up
A purchase request can be submitted only when every item has an account assignment. Test a valid request and a missing assignment, including persisted outcome after the supported save boundary. If another BO supplies a limit, double that dependency and vary its response.

Avoid this mistake
Do not label a test of a mocked Submit response as a test of Submit.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which behavior remains real?
  • How do you prove rejected data was not persisted?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines the unit/contract under test
  • Doubles only dependencies
  • Asserts state plus response semantics
Verification evidence
Show the dependency diagram and a failing test when the real Submit check is deliberately broken.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP test frameworks and boundaries
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-02 | When would SQL doubles, CDS doubles and RAP BO doubles give misleading confidence?
column2:
Short answer
They isolate different dependencies. SQL doubles replace table access, CDS doubles support tests of CDS logic, and RAP BO doubles isolate dependent EML behavior. Choose the boundary according to the risk being tested. Generic BO buffer doubles do not execute arbitrary custom provider rules, and access-control behavior needs explicit treatment. Complement isolated tests with targeted integration tests for actual persistence, authorization and service contracts.

Example and follow-up
A calculation test may use a SQL double successfully while a dependent action contract changes unnoticed. Conversely, a mocked EML response can test consumer error handling without proving the provider action. Name exactly which conclusion each test supports.

Avoid this mistake
A more sophisticated double does not automatically provide broader integration evidence.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Does this double execute custom determinations?
  • Which real boundary still needs verification?
Strong answer criteria
  • Matches doubles to dependency type
  • States excluded behavior
  • Adds focused integration evidence
Verification evidence
Record test scope and verify one representative path through the real provider and service.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP test frameworks and boundaries
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.
  • SAP transactional buffer double support
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-03 | A bulk EML action processes ten requests and rejects two. What should its test assert?
column2:
Short answer
Assert each input-to-result correlation and the intended atomicity contract, not just the number of messages. Verify which identities appear in FAILED, where reported messages point, and what changes remain buffered or persisted after transaction completion. Cover failures during interaction and save separately. The desired all-or-nothing or permitted partial-result behavior must be explicit and supported by the chosen request boundary.

Example and follow-up
Use nonsequential keys and distinct invalid reasons so accidental row-position correlation is visible. Reorder input and response fixtures. Include a successful interaction followed by a save rejection, and ensure the consumer does not report that object as durably complete.

Avoid this mistake
Do not equate ten returned messages with ten correct operation outcomes.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which failures occur only on save?
  • Can the caller correlate reordered results?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks per-instance correlation
  • Separates interaction and persistence
  • Tests the declared atomicity rule
Verification evidence
Show expected accepted/rejected identities, field messages and final persisted rows for each failure phase.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP test frameworks and boundaries
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-04 | A draft test passes when run alone but fails after another test. What would you inspect?
column2:
Short answer
Inspect shared fixtures, draft and active identities, transactional buffers, locks and double-environment lifecycle. Each test must establish its own relevant state and release/reset supported test resources. Do not use uncontrolled commits to make a suite pass. Verify draft-specific actions and the chosen test framework boundaries rather than assuming an active-instance fixture represents a draft.

Example and follow-up
Two tests reuse the same business key but differ in draft context. One leaves a buffer or configured double response behind. Run the pair in reversed order and with distinct fixtures, then fix lifecycle isolation while preserving the scenario being tested.

Avoid this mistake
A test that depends on execution order is unreliable evidence for draft behavior.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Are active and draft transactional keys distinct?
  • Which setup/teardown resource is shared?
Strong answer criteria
  • Tracks complete transactional identity
  • Resets supported resources
  • Checks ordering independence
Verification evidence
Run the isolated tests, both orders and the suite; retain evidence of deterministic results.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP test frameworks and boundaries
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-05 | How do you prove optimistic concurrency rather than merely calling the same update twice?
column2:
Short answer
Use independent consumers or sessions that read the same initial version, then perform conflicting updates in a controlled order. Assert that the first permitted write succeeds and the stale second precondition is rejected without lost data. For draft, separately test the exclusive-lock and total-ETag situations. A sequential test that rereads after every update never exercises a stale writer.

Example and follow-up
Alice and Ben read the same entity instance with its entity ETag. Alice updates that instance successfully; Ben submits an update to that same instance using the stale ETag and must not overwrite it. Separately test child-only active changes against the configured draft total ETag when resuming an expired draft lock. Keep entity-level conditional update and draft-resume concurrency assertions distinct.

Avoid this mistake
Two updates in one shared transaction are not a realistic two-user concurrency test.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do you control the interleaving?
  • Which field protects the whole draft object?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses independent contexts
  • Creates a deliberately stale request
  • Asserts unchanged data after rejection
Verification evidence
Capture request versions, responses and final values for the orchestrated conflicting sessions.

Read and verify
  • SAP total ETag and draft concurrency
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-06 | Fiori still displays an old total after a successful action. How do you separate UI refresh from backend correctness?
column2:
Short answer
Check the actual operation response and a fresh read of the authoritative BO state. If the backend value is wrong, inspect derivation triggers and transactional reads. If the backend is correct, inspect the action result, side-effect declarations, requested fields and consumer support. Avoid adding a second calculation in the UI that conceals missing backend consistency. Test the real deployed metadata rather than only a local preview.

Example and follow-up
Changing an item updates the server total but the header remains stale. Compare a direct read, a new UI session and the original session network requests. The correction may be a targeted refresh contract, not another commit or a full-page reload.

Avoid this mistake
A page reload workaround does not explain whether the backend or refresh contract was defective.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What does a fresh service read return?
  • Which request should refresh the affected property?
Strong answer criteria
  • Establishes the authoritative value
  • Traces metadata and network behavior
  • Keeps business calculation server-side
Verification evidence
Record action and follow-up reads with before/after values in the actual consumer.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP side effects
    Read the field/action trigger and refresh-target contract; verify the actual UI consumer support.

column1: OPS-07 | A RAP list becomes slow after enabling count and expanding children. What do you measure first?
column2:
Short answer
Decompose the request into data selection, total count, expansion, authorization and any ABAP or remote enrichment. Use available traces and representative parameters to measure rows, calls, database time and application time. Optimize the observed bottleneck while preserving query and security semantics. Restrict unnecessary fields or expansions where the contract permits, and verify changes with the same workload rather than an unrelated microbenchmark.

Example and follow-up
A 20-row page triggers an expensive count across millions of authorized records plus child expansion. Removing a SELECT from one handler may be irrelevant. Compare page-only, count-only and expanded requests, including a restricted user whose authorization predicate changes the plan.

Avoid this mistake
Do not optimize the shortest visible SELECT before finding the dominant request cost.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Is count more expensive than the page?
  • What changes for an authorization-restricted user?
Strong answer criteria
  • Breaks down the actual request
  • Measures representative volume and identity
  • Preserves semantics while optimizing
Verification evidence
Retain comparable request traces and latency/row/call measurements before and after the change.

Read and verify
  • SAP SQL analysis in ADT
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-08 | A custom entity calls a remote API once for every returned row. How would you remove the N+1 pattern?
column2:
Short answer
Look for supported bulk reads, selective remote filters or bounded prefetch keyed by the requested result set. Consider a governed cache or read model only with explicit freshness and scope rules. Avoid fetching the whole remote dataset to save call overhead. Propagate partial and transient failures honestly, protect credentials and tenant boundaries, and define an upper bound on work per request.

Example and follow-up
One list page of 50 items makes 51 remote calls. A bulk endpoint can retrieve the needed reference data in one request, but may return partial failures. Test missing references, duplicate keys and service throttling, not only the happy-path call count.

Avoid this mistake
An unbounded cache can trade latency for stale or cross-user data leakage.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is the maximum request size?
  • How are partial remote failures represented?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses bounded bulk access
  • Defines freshness and scope
  • Handles partial and throttled responses
Verification evidence
Measure remote-call count and transferred rows while testing missing data and rate limits.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Implementing an Unmanaged Query
    Check the supported request contract and target release. Scenario-specific bulk access and caching decisions still need their own correctness and performance evidence.

column1: OPS-09 | A service works in development but fails after transport. What evidence should the handoff have included?
column2:
Short answer
Separate transported repository artifacts from required configuration, communication setup, identities, roles, endpoint exposure and frontend deployment. Verify dependency order and the exact active source/version in the target. A published local service binding or preview in development does not establish a consumable production endpoint. The handoff should identify owners and verifiable readiness checks for each non-code dependency.

Example and follow-up
The behavior activates, but an outbound destination or communication arrangement is missing. Another issue is a target role not granting the service. Diagnose using the failure boundary and configuration evidence; do not change business code until the deployed source and configuration are reconciled.

Avoid this mistake
A green transport import is not end-to-end service acceptance.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which required items are configuration rather than source?
  • Who verifies the real consuming identity?
Strong answer criteria
  • Inventories code and configuration separately
  • Checks active target state
  • Assigns operational owners
Verification evidence
Use a target readiness checklist with actual endpoint, role, communication and smoke-test outcomes.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP service binding
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-10 | How would you evolve a released RAP service when an action needs a new mandatory input?
column2:
Short answer
Treat a new mandatory parameter as a potential breaking contract change. Assess existing consumers and choose a compatible optional/defaulted path only if its business meaning is valid; otherwise introduce a deliberate successor operation or version under the supported lifecycle. Keep old behavior operational during migration and provide deprecation guidance. Validate generated clients, metadata-driven UIs and non-UI consumers separately.

Example and follow-up
An approval action now requires a legal justification that old clients cannot supply. An empty default may violate the real business rule. Plan a transition with a measurable consumer migration target rather than silently accepting invalid data or breaking every caller at once.

Avoid this mistake
Do not call a signature change compatible merely because the server activates.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Is a default legally/business valid?
  • How do you know which consumers still use the old contract?
Strong answer criteria
  • Identifies the breaking semantic change
  • Chooses an explicit transition
  • Verifies existing consumers
Verification evidence
Run old/new consumer contract tests and track observed usage before retiring the old operation.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP service binding
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-11 | A remote approval succeeded, but the RAP caller timed out. How should an operator recover?
column2:
Short answer
Treat the outcome as uncertain until reconciled using stable correlation. Do not blindly resubmit a non-idempotent business action. Identify which system owns each committed effect and use the documented status query, idempotency contract or compensation process. Preserve a durable recovery record and route unresolved cases to an owner. A local rollback cannot erase a remote commit.

Example and follow-up
The remote workflow created an approval instance, but its response was lost. A retry should find or reuse that instance rather than create another. Include a later duplicate callback and an approval referring to an outdated local version.

Avoid this mistake
A timeout is not evidence that the other system performed no work.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is the stable correlation key?
  • Who resolves an outcome that cannot be queried?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates unknown from failed outcome
  • Reconciles before unsafe retry
  • Handles duplicate and stale callbacks
Verification evidence
Simulate lost responses and verify one intended business effect plus a visible recoverable status.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP business-object contract
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-12 | A failed save leaves no business record, but support still needs diagnostics. How would you log it safely?
column2:
Short answer
Distinguish transactional business audit data from operational diagnostics and user-facing messages. Data written in the same rolled-back transaction may disappear, while independent commits from behavior code violate transaction ownership. Use supported logging/monitoring facilities with documented lifecycle and privacy behavior. Correlate failures without exposing secrets or persisting a false successful business event.

Example and follow-up
A validation rejects an order and REPORTED provides a user message. Support needs a correlation to an observed request failure. Decide what belongs in the service/application monitoring layer and what must be saved only alongside a successful business transition.

Avoid this mistake
Do not add COMMIT WORK inside a handler just to preserve a log entry.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Should this record survive a rollback?
  • Is it diagnostic evidence or a business audit event?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates log purposes and lifetimes
  • Respects RAP completion ownership
  • Redacts sensitive diagnostic content
Verification evidence
Test success and rollback, then inspect which messages and logs survive through supported mechanisms.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP business-object contract
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-13 | A production incident starts after a release. How do you contain it without making the data worse?
column2:
Short answer
Establish affected scope, current version and the failing transaction boundary before changing code or replaying messages. Stop or limit the damaging path through authorized operational controls, preserve diagnostic evidence and assess already committed effects. Reconcile data and queues before choosing rollback, forward fix or controlled replay. A code rollback is not a general data rollback.

Example and follow-up
A new Submit action duplicates downstream approvals. Disable the affected scheduled initiation if authorized, retain correlations and identify duplicate effects. Repair idempotency and reconcile existing approvals before resuming a backlog, with a measured recovery window.

Avoid this mistake
Do not rerun the whole backlog while the duplicate-creation defect remains active.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What effects are already durable?
  • What proves it is safe to resume processing?
Strong answer criteria
  • Contains before replaying
  • Separates code from data recovery
  • Defines a measurable resume criterion
Verification evidence
Produce an incident timeline, affected-record reconciliation and a controlled post-fix replay result.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP business-object contract
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-14 | What belongs in a RAP release gate beyond a passing ATC run?
column2:
Short answer
Combine static findings with contract and behavior tests, relevant authorization cases, concurrency and rollback checks, representative performance evidence, dependency/API compatibility and target configuration readiness. Scale the gate to the changed risks. ATC can identify configured code issues but does not prove all business invariants or real integration behavior. Record unexecuted checks explicitly rather than converting missing evidence into a pass.

Example and follow-up
A change touches an action signature and an approval event. Required evidence differs from a label-only UI change: include old consumer compatibility, duplicate delivery and negative authorization. Tie each check to the relevant source revision and environment.

Avoid this mistake
A universal checklist is not a substitute for checking the risks actually changed.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which new failure mode did this change introduce?
  • Which result is pending rather than passed?
Strong answer criteria
  • Builds a risk-based gate
  • Separates static and runtime evidence
  • Records versions and pending checks
Verification evidence
Present a concise release matrix linking changed behavior to executed results, owners and remaining risks.

Read and verify

    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.
  • SAP RAP feature and release overview

column1: OPS-15 | A team advertises 95% coverage while never asserting FAILED or persisted state. How would you improve it?
column2:
Short answer
Treat coverage as a reachability signal, not proof of correct behavior. Identify critical invariants and failure modes, then add assertions that would fail if those rules were broken. Cover rejected operations, message identity, transactional cleanup and unintended side effects. Avoid adding dummy executable code or tests that merely mirror assignments. Use coverage to locate blind spots after meaningful test design.

Example and follow-up
A test executes a validation but never checks whether the invalid instance is rejected. Temporarily remove the rejection logic: if the test stays green, it does not prove the rule. Improve the assertion rather than increasing the number of similar happy-path calls.

Avoid this mistake
High statement coverage can coexist with a broken business contract.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Would the test fail if the rule were removed?
  • Which invariant is more important than the percentage?
Strong answer criteria
  • Prioritizes observable behavior
  • Uses fault-sensitive assertions
  • Reports coverage without overstating evidence
Verification evidence
Demonstrate tests that fail for deliberately broken rejection or persistence behavior, then restore the implementation.

    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.
  • SAP transactional buffer double support

column1: OPS-16 | How would you prepare an extension for a platform upgrade?
column2:
Short answer
Inventory the actual used APIs, extension contracts, classifications and target-release changes. Prioritize critical business paths and known exceptions, then run focused regression and consumer tests in a representative target environment. Verify generated metadata, authorization, draft behavior, performance and required configuration where affected. A previously released API reduces a category of risk but does not remove the need to test your own assumptions and integration.

Example and follow-up
The extension uses a classic dependency behind a wrapper and a released service consumed externally. Give each a named owner and an upgrade test strategy. A deprecated successor path may require consumer migration before the old dependency can be retired.

Avoid this mistake
Do not treat last year's clean ATC report as evidence for the new target release.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which dependencies drive the upgrade risk?
  • What behavior did your code assume beyond the documented contract?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses an actual dependency inventory
  • Tests target-specific risks
  • Tracks exception and deprecation owners
Verification evidence
Record target versions, dependency classification and regression results for the highest-impact flows.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP feature and release overview
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: OPS-17 | A cloud job processes 500,000 records and times out. How would you redesign it?
column2:
Short answer
Partition work into bounded, restartable units with stable business identities and checkpoints. Use supported background/application-job capabilities for the target environment rather than assuming classic task APIs are available. Control parallelism, database contention and remote limits. Define which units commit independently and how uncertain outcomes are reconciled. Progress reporting should distinguish processed, failed and pending items.

Example and follow-up
A pricing recalculation finishes the first 20 partitions before failure. A restart should skip safely completed work and detect conflicting newer updates. Test a crash between the business effect and checkpoint handling so the design does not rely on an unproven exactly-once assumption.

Avoid this mistake
Moving a huge synchronous loop into a background job does not solve its transaction or restart design.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is one independently recoverable unit?
  • How do newer user edits interact with retry?
Strong answer criteria
  • Bounds work and contention
  • Defines durable restart semantics
  • Uses supported cloud execution APIs
Verification evidence
Inject mid-partition failures and verify recovery, resource limits and final reconciliation.

Read and verify
  • SAP application job catalog and template
    Read the supported job execution model, then design bounded units and restart checkpoints for the workload.

column1: OPS-18 | How would you communicate senior readiness when you can review code locally but cannot run SAP checks?
column2:
Short answer
Separate what was inspected, prepared and actually executed. A local source review can identify contract defects and propose tests, but cannot establish activation, real authorization, ATC results or measured SAP runtime behavior. Provide a precise target execution handoff with expected outcomes and dependencies. This is stronger evidence than inventing a pass or quoting performance numbers from a different environment.

Example and follow-up
For a RAP approval change, supply positive/negative EML cases, a two-session concurrency script, role prerequisites and a service smoke test. State the relevant source revision and what must be returned from the target before claiming acceptance.

Avoid this mistake
Do not present prepared test code or a mocked UI as successful SAP integration.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which claim can you prove now?
  • What exact target result would close the remaining risk?
Strong answer criteria
  • Labels evidence honestly
  • Gives executable acceptance scenarios
  • Ties results to source and environment
Verification evidence
Provide a prepared/executed/pending matrix with specific acceptance criteria and accountable owners.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP test frameworks and boundaries
    Use the framework contract to design the proposed evidence; no runtime result is claimed here.

column1: GOV-01 | A project claims Level A because its frontend uses RAP. How would you assess the extension?
column2:
Short answer
I would define the assessment scope and inspect the actual dependency and extension paths, including adapters and called custom code. Level A relies on released contracts and the relevant supported development approach; Level B uses classified classic APIs, Level C internal objects, and Level D non-recommended dependencies or techniques. RAP or a Fiori frontend does not determine the classification alone. I would record object-level evidence and avoid presenting a mixed solution as uniformly Level A.

Example and follow-up
A RAP handler may call a customer wrapper that ultimately invokes an internal SAP object. The consumer boundary and wrapper can require separate assessment, but the delivery still contains that exposure. A useful report links each finding to the affected business capability and responsible owner, rather than counting only visible service artifacts.

Avoid this mistake
RAP, BTP deployment, a customer namespace, or a green UI test is not proof that every underlying dependency is Level A.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What exactly is included in the claimed Level A scope?
  • How would you find dependencies hidden behind customer adapters?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines scope before classification
  • Traces indirect dependencies
  • Separates framework choice from API evidence
Verification evidence
An object-level dependency inventory with target-system release/classification evidence and the applicable ATC result for the same revision.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core levels, classic APIs, wrappers, and edition boundaries
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-02 | An API is released with C1. A team assumes that means Clean Core Level C and permission to expose it remotely. How do you respond?
column2:
Short answer
I would separate the naming systems. C0 is the Extend release contract, C1 is Use System-Internally, and C2 is Use as Remote API; these are purposes and stability contracts, not Clean Core A-D categories. A C1 release must also have the appropriate visibility for its consumer. Remote exposure needs a supported remote contract and communication design. I would inspect the object's API state and documented use rather than infer permissions from the letter C.

Example and follow-up
A local released class can support an on-stack application without being a remote API itself. Building a custom remote service around it creates a new owned contract with authentication, authorization, error semantics, and lifecycle obligations. It does not magically convert the underlying object to C2 or inherit every provider guarantee.

Avoid this mistake
C0/C1/C2 and Clean Core A/B/C/D are different classifications; release for one purpose does not release every possible usage.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which visibility must the API expose for this caller?
  • What responsibilities arise if you build a custom remote service over a local API?
Strong answer criteria
  • Names contracts accurately
  • Checks purpose and visibility
  • Recognizes new provider responsibilities
Verification evidence
ADT API-state properties, provider documentation, and a consumer design showing local use or an explicitly owned remote contract.

Read and verify
  • SAP release contracts, visibility, and API lifecycle states
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-03 | A team wraps an internal SAP function module and releases the wrapper. Has the technical debt disappeared?
column2:
Short answer
No. A wrapper can isolate callers, translate contracts, and create a replaceable boundary, but it does not change the release status or upgrade exposure of its underlying dependency. I would record both the consumer's contract and the wrapper's implementation risk. Where classic boundaries are allowed, the wrapper needs an owner, regression tests, target-release assessment, and an exit plan. I would also question whether the wrapper adds useful isolation or merely renames the same unstable interface.

Example and follow-up
If the wrapper publishes the internal function's structures unchanged, a provider change can still propagate directly to every consumer. A narrower application contract can contain that change. SAP's current level guidance includes wrappers over classified classic APIs in Level B scope; wrapping an internal object does not make that dependency classified classic.

Avoid this mistake
A customer release flag does not turn an unreleased SAP dependency into a released SAP API or erase its classification.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which unstable details must stay behind the wrapper?
  • Who replaces the dependency when a released alternative becomes available?
Strong answer criteria
  • Tracks underlying exposure
  • Designs a narrow stable boundary
  • Assigns replacement ownership
Verification evidence
A wrapper dependency record, contract tests, an owner, and a documented replacement trigger with the current target-release assessment.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core levels, classic APIs, wrappers, and edition boundaries
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-04 | An urgent release needs an ATC exemption for an internal dependency. What makes the exception governable?
column2:
Short answer
I would require a specific business need, exact finding and source scope, target edition, alternatives considered, risk owner, and compensating verification. The exception should have an expiry or review trigger and a funded remediation path, not an indefinite blanket waiver. An ATC exemption changes handling of a finding; it does not make unsupported syntax legal, change SAP's API contract, or establish business correctness. The release decision must explicitly accept the residual exposure.

Example and follow-up
An exception for one read-only adapter should not silently cover additional write calls introduced later. Tie it to the relevant objects and finding category, rerun checks after changes, and require review when the target release or provider changes. Security and transactional defects need their own assessment rather than being bundled into a clean-core waiver.

Avoid this mistake
An approved exemption is not a reclassification to Level A and must not become a general permission to bypass ABAP Cloud restrictions.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What event invalidates this exception?
  • How do you prevent the approved scope from growing unnoticed?
Strong answer criteria
  • Bounds scope and lifetime
  • Names accountable risk ownership
  • Separates exemption from technical permission
Verification evidence
An exception record linked to the exact ATC finding, source revision, release target, regression evidence, owner, and expiry or review trigger.

Read and verify
  • SAP ATC configuration and transport-release governance
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-05 | A Level B solution works in Private Edition. Can the same approval justify deploying it in Public Edition?
column2:
Short answer
No. Clean Core classification does not override the target product's available development model, APIs, or extension mechanisms. I would reassess the requirement against Public Edition's supported configuration, key-user and developer extensibility, and remote integration options. A classified classic API acceptable in a private-edition context may not be available there. The governance record should describe that portability gap openly and compare a supported redesign with retaining the current deployment for a justified business reason.

Example and follow-up
A classic enhancement or SAP GUI-dependent component may have a stable role in an existing private-edition application but no permitted equivalent in the proposed public-cloud scope. Moving only its UI to BTP does not restore access to an unavailable backend API. Validate the actual business operation end to end.

Avoid this mistake
Level B is not a universal deployment permission, and Level A design does not guarantee identical API coverage across editions.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which part of the solution is genuinely portable?
  • What evidence would justify keeping a private-edition dependency?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks target-edition constraints
  • Separates classification from portability
  • Offers supported redesign options
Verification evidence
An edition capability comparison with verified target APIs, extension points, and a documented functional gap for each nonportable component.

Read and verify
  • SAP extensibility options by environment and language version
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-06 | You have thousands of custom objects and a limited upgrade budget. How would you prioritize remediation?
column2:
Short answer
I would combine usage evidence, business criticality, dependency classification, known target-release changes, and remediation effort. Unused objects may be retirement candidates after validating completeness of the observation window. High-impact Level D or changed internal dependencies usually warrant early investigation, while stable low-risk dependencies can follow a planned backlog. Object counts alone are misleading: one heavily used posting dependency can matter more than hundreds of harmless utilities. Each prioritized item needs an owner and acceptance criteria.

Example and follow-up
A year-end report can look unused during a three-month trace window. Deleting it based only on that sample would create a business outage. Conversely, a rarely executed emergency posting tool may still have high operational criticality. Combine telemetry with process-owner confirmation and target-upgrade impact analysis.

Avoid this mistake
Do not equate low execution frequency with low business importance or treat every finding as equal remediation work.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you avoid retiring seasonal functionality?
  • What makes one Level C dependency more urgent than another?
Strong answer criteria
  • Combines usage and business impact
  • Uses target-release change evidence
  • Prioritizes actionable owned work
Verification evidence
A ranked remediation portfolio with usage-window limitations, business-owner decisions, dependency impact, estimated effort, and target-release tests.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core levels, classic APIs, wrappers, and edition boundaries
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-07 | No released API supports a required business operation. What would your escalation contain?
column2:
Short answer
I would describe the business outcome, target product and release, required operation and transaction semantics, expected volume, and the precise missing capability. I would document searched APIs and extension points, explain why standard configuration or a remote alternative does not fit, and provide a minimal reproducible example where useful. The escalation should support an actionable provider decision while the project evaluates a bounded process change, delayed scope, or an edition-appropriate governed alternative.

Example and follow-up
Saying 'please release this table' may prescribe a fragile implementation rather than explain the need. A request for a supported command to close a document, including authorization, validation, and failure semantics, gives the provider a clearer requirement. Any interim workaround still needs its own risk and retirement record.

Avoid this mistake
An API-gap ticket does not authorize direct table access or promise that the requested API will arrive by the project's deadline.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What evidence shows that existing APIs really do not fit?
  • How do you keep delivery moving without hiding the gap?
Strong answer criteria
  • Escalates a business capability
  • Documents rejected supported alternatives
  • Defines an explicit interim plan
Verification evidence
A capability-gap dossier with release-specific API searches, required semantics, a reproducible scenario, and a decision on interim scope.

Read and verify
  • SAP extensibility options by environment and language version
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-08 | The business asks to reproduce a heavily customized legacy process exactly. How do you challenge that without dismissing the requirement?
column2:
Short answer
I would separate mandatory business outcomes from historical implementation choices, then demonstrate how standard configuration and supported extensions meet each outcome. Legal, contractual, and differentiating requirements deserve explicit evidence; familiar screen sequences alone may not. I would quantify the cost of preserving deviations, including upgrade tests and operations, and compare a smaller supported extension or process adjustment. The business owner should decide with concrete examples of retained value, changed behavior, and residual risk.

Example and follow-up
A legacy approval screen might combine fields that standard applications split across steps, while the actual control requirement is segregation of duties and an auditable decision. Recreating the old screen through internal hooks can add risk without preserving additional value. A process walkthrough should expose exceptions, not only the happy path.

Avoid this mistake
Fit-to-standard is not a slogan for refusing real requirements, and exact visual parity is not always the real business invariant.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which requirement is mandatory and who can prove it?
  • What exception case could invalidate the proposed standard process?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates outcomes from historical design
  • Uses concrete process demonstrations
  • Makes cost and ownership visible
Verification evidence
A fit-gap matrix with business-owner acceptance, exception-path demonstrations, and lifecycle cost estimates for retained deviations.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core dimensions beyond extensions
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-09 | Your team wants to release a custom API used by three other teams. What must be ready before setting its release state?
column2:
Short answer
I would require a deliberate public surface, supported use cases, error and transaction semantics, authorization expectations, and a named owner prepared to maintain compatibility. Consumers need stable types and behavior, not leaked persistence details. I would capture a delivered API baseline, configure applicable compatibility checks, and define deprecation and successor policies. If the interface is still experimental and coordinated internal reuse is sufficient, a supported component-access arrangement may be more honest than a premature stability promise.

Example and follow-up
Removing an optional field or changing a rounding rule can break a consumer even if the developer considers it cleanup. Compatibility snapshots help detect relevant technical changes, while consumer tests protect business semantics. Do not regenerate the baseline merely to silence findings from an incompatible change to a delivered contract.

Avoid this mistake
Releasing an API is a provider commitment; broad access permission is not equivalent to a stable contract.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which changes can be detected statically and which need consumer tests?
  • How would you deprecate the API without breaking current users?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines provider obligations
  • Protects delivered baselines
  • Combines technical and semantic checks
Verification evidence
An API specification, owner and consumer list, prior-delivery snapshot, compatibility results, and consumer-contract test evidence.

Read and verify
  • SAP release contracts, visibility, and API lifecycle states
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.
  • SAP software component dependencies and compatibility snapshots
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-10 | The direct dependency scan is clean, but an upgrade still breaks the extension. What could the governance model be missing?
column2:
Short answer
I would inspect indirect custom dependencies, dynamic calls, configuration-selected implementations, remote contracts, and data assumptions outside the scanned scope. A scan can also miss relevant objects if its package selection, check version, or classification data is incomplete. I would connect findings to a dependency graph and process-level tests, recording evidence limitations. Clean direct references are useful, but they do not establish that every runtime path or semantic assumption is protected against the target change.

Example and follow-up
A custom facade may select an internal implementation through configuration, or a remote service may change independently of the ABAP transport. Another failure can come from expecting one text row where new data produces several. The graph must include configuration and integration edges, with accountable owners and representative runtime coverage.

Avoid this mistake
A green direct-reference check is not proof that the whole solution has no unsupported or semantically fragile dependencies.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you discover configuration-driven dependencies?
  • Which runtime paths must the upgrade rehearsal cover?
Strong answer criteria
  • Explores indirect and dynamic edges
  • Questions scan completeness
  • Adds process-level verification
Verification evidence
An expanded dependency graph, documented scan scope and tool versions, and upgrade regression evidence covering configured runtime paths.

Read and verify
  • SAP software component relations and consistency checks
    Check classification, release scope and governance separately.

column1: GOV-11 | How would you enforce Clean Core in delivery without blocking every legacy transport immediately?
column2:
Short answer
I would establish a trustworthy baseline, prevent new unapproved exposure, and prioritize remediation of existing risk through owned work. Gates should use the applicable language checks, API and enhancement checks, compatibility checks, and security or correctness tests for the target environment. Existing exceptions need bounded review rather than silent suppression. I would record the variant, priorities, scope, and baseline policy so a green gate has a reproducible meaning and developers receive feedback before release day.

Example and follow-up
A transport that changes a legacy report's layout should not automatically trigger an unplanned rewrite of the entire application, but it also must not introduce a new internal write dependency unnoticed. Separate unchanged baseline exposure from new findings, then require review when an edit changes the risk of an existing exception.

Avoid this mistake
A baseline is not approval for unlimited new debt, and transport blocking thresholds are configured policy rather than a universal property of every ATC check.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What happens when a touched legacy dependency becomes riskier?
  • How do you stop teams from weakening the shared check variant?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes baseline from new risk
  • Uses reproducible early gates
  • Governs exception and policy changes
Verification evidence
A versioned gate policy, representative pass/fail cases, a protected check-configuration record, and a baseline-to-current findings comparison.

column1: GOV-12 | A vendor upgrade changes an object used by an approved Level C extension. How do you organize the response?
column2:
Short answer
I would identify affected consumers and business processes, compare the old and new provider behavior, and determine whether a released alternative now exists. The approved exception should trigger reassessment for this target release. I would reproduce the failure in an upgrade environment, adapt the isolated boundary if still justified, and run focused integration and regression tests. Delivery must coordinate vendor and customer changes, with rollback or business recovery defined for persistence or contract changes.

Example and follow-up
An internal object's unchanged signature can conceal different defaulting or validation behavior. Conversely, an activation failure may reveal a straightforward type change. Both require more than a syntax fix: test postings, authorizations, messages, and affected data transitions against the intended business outcome, using the actual upgraded system revision.

Avoid this mistake
A previous exception or successful prior upgrade does not prove compatibility with the next vendor release.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do you distinguish an API change from a data-dependent defect?
  • Would you keep the exception if a suitable released successor is now available?
Strong answer criteria
  • Reassesses release-specific exposure
  • Tests semantic behavior
  • Coordinates recovery and replacement
Verification evidence
A target-upgrade impact record, reproduced failure, reviewed boundary change, and process regression results tied to both vendor and custom revisions.

column1: GOV-13 | What would a credible two-year custom-code modernization roadmap look like?
column2:
Short answer
I would organize the roadmap by business capability and lifecycle risk, with early retirement of confirmed unused functionality and focused replacement of high-exposure dependencies. New development should follow supported ABAP Cloud contracts where suitable, while valuable classic capabilities can coexist under explicit governance. Each phase needs measurable outcomes, owners, dependencies, and operational acceptance. The roadmap must reserve capacity for API changes and upgrades rather than promise that every object will be rewritten in RAP by a fixed date.

Example and follow-up
One phase might remove an unused interface, another replace internal reads with a released query, and another redesign a transaction that owns an unstable posting path. These changes produce different benefits and require different tests. Counting converted classes alone can reward cosmetic work while leaving the highest-risk dependency untouched.

Avoid this mistake
Modernization is not measured reliably by RAP object count or by replacing all classic code regardless of business value.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What quarterly outcome would demonstrate reduced upgrade risk?
  • How do you fund remediation that has no visible new UI feature?
Strong answer criteria
  • Prioritizes capability outcomes
  • Preserves justified coexistence
  • Uses measurable risk reduction
Verification evidence
A capability-based roadmap with owners, usage decisions, target dependency reductions, migration acceptance criteria, and budgeted upgrade work.

column1: GOV-14 | A classified classic API meets the need, while a released API covers only half the operation. Would you accept Level B?
column2:
Short answer
In a target environment that permits the classic approach, I would compare the supported business completeness and lifecycle risk of both options. A properly classified Level B API can be a defensible choice; it is not automatically a defect to rewrite. I would verify that the complete dependency path and extension technique qualify, avoid misleading Level A claims, and preserve a migration option. The decision must not override Public Edition or ABAP Cloud language restrictions.

Example and follow-up
Splitting one business operation across an incomplete released API and direct table updates can be worse than using a complete classified classic business API. The comparison should include transaction integrity, supported fields, authorization, maintainability, and future product direction. Confirm classification of the specific object instead of generalizing from the word BAPI.

Avoid this mistake
Not every old API is Level B, and a Level B assessment does not make it directly callable from restricted ABAP Cloud code.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What makes the exact API qualify as classic rather than internal?
  • What would cause you to revisit this decision after an upgrade?
Strong answer criteria
  • Makes an evidence-based B decision
  • Preserves transaction completeness
  • Respects target and language constraints
Verification evidence
Specific object-classification evidence, a complete operation test, a comparison with released alternatives, and a scheduled reassessment trigger.

column1: GOV-15 | A required report uses an internal read object with no current replacement. Would you accept Level C, and under what conditions?
column2:
Short answer
I would first verify the actual gap, data semantics, authorization, and deployment constraints. If a permitted Level C dependency remains necessary, I would isolate its use, limit the public contract, record the target-release exposure, and assign an owner for provider changes and replacement. Read-only access lowers some transaction risks but does not eliminate confidentiality, correctness, or upgrade risk. Acceptance should be specific, time-bounded or trigger-bound, and supported by representative result and authorization tests.

Example and follow-up
An internal view may change filtering or joins without causing a syntax error, yielding duplicate rows or exposing unintended data. A regression fixture should check business totals, row identity, and denied access, not merely successful execution. Where release-specific change information is available, use it as an input rather than a complete compatibility guarantee.

Avoid this mistake
Read-only does not mean risk-free, and Level C is not a blanket exemption for all internal objects or non-recommended Level D techniques.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What result change could escape an activation check?
  • Which precise event forces this exception back into review?
Strong answer criteria
  • Treats read semantics as consequential
  • Isolates and owns exposure
  • Defines focused compatibility evidence
Verification evidence
A bounded exception with dependency classification, authorization and result baselines, target-upgrade checks, and replacement-review triggers.

column1: GOV-16 | How would you assess a solution that uses a released CDS query, a classified classic BAPI, an internal class, and a modification?
column2:
Short answer
I would assess the four paths separately and confirm their actual usage and applicable classifications on the target system. The released query can support Level A use when consumed under the right contract; the classified classic API introduces Level B scope, the internal dependency Level C scope, and a non-recommended modification can introduce Level D exposure. I would not average these into a reassuring score. I would identify affected capabilities, alternatives, criticality, and the highest-risk remediation first.

Example and follow-up
The modification may be in an unused historical path, while the internal class supports daily financial posting. Both facts matter to sequencing, but neither changes the factual dependency record. Removal requires usage validation and process-owner approval; replacing a dependency requires proving the same intended business operation and error behavior.

Avoid this mistake
A single letter for a mixed solution can hide scope; classification and remediation priority are related but are not the same decision.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which capability would you remediate first and why?
  • What evidence is required before removing the modification?
Strong answer criteria
  • Classifies paths rather than averages
  • Separates exposure from priority
  • Uses business and usage evidence
Verification evidence
A scoped assessment table linking each dependency to classification evidence, process impact, usage, ownership, and a justified remediation decision.

column1: GOV-17 | The sponsor says Clean Core is a developer concern and rejects funding for integration monitoring and data cleanup. How would you negotiate?
column2:
Short answer
I would connect the proposal to operational and business outcomes: failed interfaces, unreliable master data, unsupported software, and complex process variants can prevent safe upgrades even when custom code is well structured. Clean Core includes more than extension code. I would present concrete incidents or scenario costs, propose a minimum owned control set, and distinguish mandatory controls from improvements that can be phased. The sponsor should explicitly decide which residual business risks remain and who operates them.

Example and follow-up
A technically released order API still fails repeatedly when customer mappings are invalid and nobody owns the error queue. Developers cannot solve that through an ATC exemption or another wrapper. A practical agreement assigns mapping ownership, alert response, reconciliation, and cleanup priorities with measurable service expectations.

Avoid this mistake
A strong extensibility classification does not certify clean data, standard processes, secure integrations, or effective operations.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which control delivers the highest near-term business value?
  • Who is accountable when an interface remains technically successful but business processing is incomplete?
Strong answer criteria
  • Connects non-code controls to outcomes
  • Negotiates proportional phased scope
  • Assigns business and operational ownership
Verification evidence
A responsibility matrix, costed minimum control plan, measurable operational targets, and documented acceptance of deferred risks.

column1: GOV-18 | An interview panel shows an A-D chart with ATC priorities. What would you clarify before treating it as a release gate?
column2:
Short answer
I would explain the chart's intended check context, then ask which variant, check implementations, priorities, classification data, object scope, and target release produced the findings. A mapping used by an API-usage check is not a universal meaning of every ATC priority. Other findings can concern security, correctness, or performance. A clean-core gate should preserve that distinction and state what a pass proves, what exemptions exist, and which runtime evidence remains necessary.

Example and follow-up
Two projects can show different findings because one omitted an enhancement check or used older classification data, not because its code is cleaner. Even a matching configuration cannot prove business transaction correctness. Save the run metadata and compare like-for-like scopes before using counts or severity trends in a management dashboard.

Avoid this mistake
Do not interpret every priority 1 finding as Level D, every priority 2 as Level C, or absence of findings as proof of complete Level A coverage.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What would you store so this assessment can be reproduced?
  • How would you distinguish an exempted finding from a resolved dependency?
Strong answer criteria
  • Qualifies severity mapping by check
  • Requires reproducible assessment scope
  • Separates static findings from runtime proof
Verification evidence
The exact ATC variant and check configuration, classification/version information, source and scope identifiers, exemptions, and complementary runtime validation results.
